profile.title: Prediabetes, Obesity, and Anemia in a Reserved Caregiver: First Nutrition Counseling Visit
profile.summary: A 43-year-old woman with prediabetes, obesity, and anemia presents for a first telehealth nutrition counseling visit, precise about her lab numbers but initially guarded about the caregiving burden and meal-skipping behind her takeaway-heavy eating pattern. The case teaches eliciting psychosocial barriers behind a reserved presentation, connecting labs/symptoms to a concrete first behavior change at the patient's stage of change, and recognizing a mismatch between a stated explanation (schedule) and the fuller picture revealed through rapport-building (caregiving duties, inconsistent iron supplement use).
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in Bloomfield, New Jersey, seated at her kitchen table
profile.encounterType: nutrition assessment and counseling (initial telehealth visit)

patient.name: María Eugenia Rosas
patient.occupation: Billing coordinator at a dental office
patient.language: Spanish (primary), English (second language, used for work and most medical visits)
patient.appearance: Seated at a small kitchen table at home, dressed in work clothes as if just off a shift. Posture upright and composed, pale conjunctiva visible on camera, flattened affect that becomes more noticeable as the conversation goes on. Keeps a small notebook next to her laptop.

persona.personality: Reserved and private; precise and detail-oriented about clinical facts; warms up slowly once she senses she will not be judged
persona.communicationStyle: Gives short, factual answers to open-ended questions initially; cites exact lab values and dates from memory; dislikes vague advice and responds better to specific, concrete suggestions; may deflect personal questions by returning to a number or date
persona.emotionalState: Guarded but motivated; underlying worry about progressing to diabetes; some fatigue-related flatness by the end of a longer conversation
persona.background: Grew up in a bilingual household where food was never the center of elaborate home cooking; her mother worked long shifts and takeaway or quick plates from neighborhood spots became the norm. Now works full-time as a billing coordinator at a dental office and lives in a household of eight with extended family. Keeps a notebook of her lab numbers after every visit. Has a cousin in a similar weight management program she sometimes compares notes with. Prefers tea in the evening but rarely has time to make it.
speechExamples: My A1C was 6.2% as of April 24th, and my glucose was 64.6.
I don't really want a whole overhaul, I just want one specific thing to start with.
I eat out most days, it's just how my schedule works.
I guess I only take the iron pills sometimes, when I remember.
It's not laziness, there's just... a lot going on at home.
concerns: Worried prediabetes will become full diabetes like it did for her aunt
Concerned about her low hemoglobin and whether it's connected to how tired she feels
Frustrated that her schedule leaves no room to cook

scenario.studentBrief: You are joining a telehealth video visit with María Eugenia Rosas, a 43-year-old woman referred for nutrition counseling after recent labs flagged prediabetes, obesity, and anemia. This is her first visit with you. Review the available chart information before the call, then conduct a nutrition-focused assessment and counseling session.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for nutrition counseling after labs showing prediabetes, obesity, and anemia
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for seeing me. My doctor sent me here because of my last labs - my A1C was 6.2% and my BMI was just over 30. I figured I should get this handled before it turns into something worse.
tasks: Take a focused nutrition and social history of the presenting concern
Review relevant anthropometric and laboratory data with the patient and connect it to her symptoms
Identify barriers affecting her eating pattern and self-care using patient-centered, non-judgmental questions
Collaboratively identify one concrete, feasible first behavior change consistent with her stated goals
Document the encounter using the ADIME format

facts.chart: Referred for nutrition counseling after labs showing HbA1c 6.2%, hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, and BMI 30.1
facts.says: My doctor sent me here because my last labs showed my A1C was 6.2% and my iron was low again. They said my BMI was just over 30.

facts.chart: Reports fatigue most afternoons after 3pm
facts.says: I get really tired most afternoons, especially after 3pm. It's hard to focus by then.

facts.chart: Reports eating out or ordering takeaway 5-6 days a week due to work schedule
facts.says: I eat out most days, honestly. My schedule just doesn't leave time to cook.

facts.chart: Reports shortness of breath climbing stairs at work
facts.says: I get short of breath going up the stairs at my office. It didn't used to be like that.

facts.chart: Reports increased thirst compared to baseline
facts.says: I've noticed I'm thirstier than I used to be, actually.

facts.chart: Reports occasional lightheadedness, attributes to anemia
facts.says: Sometimes I get a little lightheaded. I figure that's just my low iron.

facts.chart: Describes usual lunch order as rotisserie chicken plate with rice from a restaurant near work
facts.says: For lunch I usually get a rotisserie chicken plate with rice from the place next to my office. I don't really measure it, I just get what looks like a normal plate.

facts.chart: Describes evening meals as pupusas or empanadas from a nearby stand on weeknights, or takeaway; home-cooked meal only on Sundays
facts.says: On weeknights I usually grab pupusas or empanadas from a stand near my place, I'm too tired to cook. Sundays are the only day the whole house eats something homemade together.

facts.chart: Reports breakfast is usually coffee with condensed milk, sometimes a bread roll
facts.says: In the morning I just have coffee, sweet, with condensed milk. Sometimes a roll if I have time.

facts.chart: Reports diet soda with most meals and inconsistent water intake
facts.says: I drink diet soda with most meals. Water I kind of forget until I'm really thirsty.

facts.chart: Reports taking OTC iron tablets inconsistently, 'when I remember'
facts.says: I have iron tablets, but honestly I only take them sometimes, when I remember.

facts.chart: Takes a multivitamin recommended by a family member; keeps ginger candies at desk for nausea
facts.says: I also take a multivitamin my cousin recommended, and I keep ginger candies at my desk if my stomach feels off.

facts.chart: Lives in a household of 8 with extended family
facts.says: There are eight of us in the house, it's a big household.

facts.chart: Discloses spending several hours after work caring for an elderly relative in the household, leaving little personal time
facts.says: After work I'm usually taking care of my grandmother for a few hours most nights. There isn't a lot left for me by the time that's done.

facts.chart: Clarifies that caregiving responsibilities, not lack of effort, are the main barrier to cooking at home
facts.says: It's not that I don't want to cook more. It's that by the time I'm done helping my grandmother, there's just no time or energy left.

facts.chart: Reports skipping her own lunch on some days to finish caregiving tasks before a relative's appointments
facts.says: Some days I actually skip my own lunch so I can get my grandmother ready in time for her appointments. I haven't really told anyone that.

facts.chart: Expresses guilt about skipping meals for caregiving duties
facts.says: I feel kind of guilty about it, skipping meals like that. It's not really something I bring up.

facts.chart: Reports a missed medical appointment due to lack of reliable transportation
facts.says: I actually missed an appointment once because I couldn't get a ride and the bus schedule didn't line up.

facts.chart: Reports family minimizes her prediabetes and anemia diagnoses
facts.says: My family kind of brushes it off, like it's nothing serious. They don't really get why I'm worried.

facts.chart: Describes family gatherings as centered on heavy, convenience-based meals that have not changed since her diagnoses
facts.says: When we all get together it's the same heavy food as always, nothing's really changed just because of my labs.

facts.chart: Self-reports quite a bit of stress
facts.says: I'd say I have quite a bit of stress, yeah.

facts.chart: States preference for one specific, concrete first step rather than a broad diet overhaul
facts.says: I don't want some big overhaul. I just want one specific thing I can start doing this week.

facts.chart: States goal of lowering next HbA1c result
facts.says: I want my next A1C to come back lower than 6.2.

facts.chart: States goal of having more energy through the full workday
facts.says: I just want enough energy to get through my whole workday without crashing.

facts.chart: Expresses fear of progressing to type 2 diabetes, citing an aunt's history
facts.says: My aunt went from prediabetes to full diabetes. I really don't want that to happen to me.

facts.chart: Believes fatigue is due to anemia alone, not related to diet pattern
facts.says: I just figured the tiredness is from the anemia, not really connected to what I'm eating.

facts.chart: Believes cooking more at home mainly requires more willpower
facts.says: I think I just need more willpower to cook more, honestly.

facts.chart: Does not drink alcohol, AUDIT-C score 0
facts.says: I don't drink at all.

facts.chart: Does not smoke
facts.says: I've never smoked.

facts.chart: Reports walking to bus stop and around office; no structured exercise, cites lack of time
facts.says: I walk to the bus stop and around the office, that's about it. There's just no time for a real workout.

facts.chart: Reports approximately 6 hours of sleep most nights, often interrupted
facts.says: I get about six hours most nights, and it's not always straight through.

facts.chart: Reports socializing outside the home only 1-2 times a week
facts.says: I only really see people outside the house maybe once or twice a week.

facts.chart: History of whiplash injury to neck, 2026-07 to 2026-09, resolved, with physical and occupational therapy
facts.says: I had a whiplash injury a while back and did some physical therapy for it, but that's all cleared up now.

facts.chart: History of severe anxiety/panic, 2017 to 2025, resolved
facts.says: I used to deal with pretty bad anxiety, panic attacks and all, but that resolved a while back.

facts.chart: History of tubal ligation since 2008
facts.says: I had my tubes tied back in 2008.

objectives.text: Elicit a full social and caregiving history behind a reserved presentation, including household composition, caregiving duties, and transportation barriers
Translate lab values and clinical facts into a single, concrete, patient-centered first behavior change consistent with the preparation stage of change
Explore the relationship between anemia, fatigue, and dietary pattern, including supplement adherence and iron-rich food intake
Address family dynamics that undermine health goals without blaming the family
Problem-solve around the transportation barrier and caregiving-related meal skipping, and identify its effect on care continuity and nutrition status
Identify and gently explore a discrepancy between a patient's stated explanation for a behavior and corroborating record evidence, without breaking rapport

answerKey.primaryProblem: Altered nutrition-related laboratory values (prediabetes, HbA1c 6.2%) and excess energy intake related to a takeaway-dominant eating pattern and caregiving-related meal skipping, as evidenced by elevated HbA1c, BMI 30.1, and self-reported skipped lunches
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive energy intake related to frequent high-portion takeaway meals and sugar-sweetened beverages as evidenced by BMI 30.1 and HbA1c 6.2%
Nutrition diagnosis: Inadequate iron intake related to limited intake of iron-rich foods and inconsistent supplement adherence as evidenced by hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL and reported fatigue
Nutrition diagnosis: Limited access to self-care/food preparation related to caregiving burden and household demands as evidenced by reported skipped meals and lack of time to cook
Alternative consideration: Fatigue attributable solely to anemia without dietary contribution (patient's own belief, to be explored and gently reframed)
keyFindings: HbA1c 6.2% (prediabetes range) with BMI 30.1 kg/m2 and 2.0 kg weight gain since 2023
Hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL (low) with inconsistent OTC iron supplement adherence and low iron-rich food intake
Eating pattern dominated by takeaway/convenience foods 5-6 days/week, sugar-sweetened coffee and diet soda, inconsistent water intake
Hidden caregiving burden (several hours/evening caring for elderly relative) and occasional self-skipped lunches, with associated guilt
Transportation barrier previously causing a missed appointment; family minimizes her diagnoses and continues serving heavy convenience foods at gatherings
Patient is in the preparation stage of change and wants one concrete, specific first step rather than a broad overhaul
plan: Collaboratively select one concrete, feasible first behavior change (e.g., modifying an existing takeaway order, such as swapping diet soda for water at one meal, or adding an iron-rich side to her usual lunch order)
Provide specific, non-judgmental education linking dietary pattern to both glycemic risk and anemia/fatigue, correcting the belief that fatigue is 'just the anemia'
Address iron supplement adherence barriers directly and suggest a simple reminder strategy (e.g., pairing with an existing habit like morning coffee)
Discuss practical, low-burden ways to preserve her own lunch during caregiving-heavy days (e.g., a portable iron-rich snack kept on hand)
Validate the caregiving burden and family dynamics without criticizing family; explore any community or respite resources she may be open to
Discuss telehealth as a strategy to maintain follow-up continuity given the transportation barrier
Plan follow-up visit to recheck HbA1c and hemoglobin trend and reassess progress on the chosen behavior change
redFlags: Hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL with ongoing fatigue, lightheadedness, and exertional shortness of breath warrants communication with referring physician if symptoms worsen or hemoglobin trends further down
Self-reported meal skipping tied to caregiving burden with associated guilt, which could affect both nutritional status and mental well-being if unaddressed
Family minimization of diagnoses and ongoing transportation barriers may limit follow-through on any plan without problem-solving support
educationPoints: HbA1c of 6.2% falls in the prediabetes range (5.7-6.4%) and is modifiable with dietary pattern changes
Dietary pattern (frequency, portions, beverage choices) can influence both glycemic control and energy balance even when individual lab values like lipids are currently normal
Iron-rich food intake and consistent supplement use both matter for correcting anemia; sporadic supplement use alone is unlikely to normalize hemoglobin
Fatigue can have multiple contributing factors (anemia, meal skipping, sleep, stress) rather than a single cause

Small, specific, sustainable changes within an existing eating pattern (e.g., modifying a usual order) are often more achievable than a full dietary overhaul, especially in the preparation stage of change

mismatches.patientClaim: Reports taking her OTC iron tablets sometimes, when she remembers
mismatches.recordEvidence: Referral note documents patient reports intermittent use of over-the-counter iron supplement, consistent with ongoing low hemoglobin of 11.7 g/dL despite supplementation being recommended
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported intermittent adherence to an iron supplement correlates with a persistently low hemoglobin; explore adherence barriers rather than assuming the supplement alone will correct anemia, and assess dietary iron intake as an adjunct.
